extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, in-house counsel, and clients interested in design patent damages
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating which 'article of manufacture' is the proper unit for §289 damages in design-patent infringement and methods for calculating the infringer's profits attributable to that article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory scope of design patents (35 U.S.C. §171)
rubrics_metrics.description: A design patent protects “any new, original and ornamental design for an article of manufacture.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with utility patents (35 U.S.C. §101) which protect functional inventions. Design patents are limited to ornamental aspects applied to an article of manufacture; identifying the ornamental design is prerequisite to locating the relevant article-of-manufacture for damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages under 35 U.S.C. §289
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 289 permits an owner to recover the infringer’s total profit from the article of manufacture to which the patented design was applied, but not less than $250.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted statutory language emphasizes recovery 'to the extent of his total profit, but not less than $250.' The statute also states it shall not prevent other remedies but prohibits recovering the profit twice. This statutory framework drives whether courts award total product profits or require a narrower focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article-of-manufacture two-step analysis (Article of Manufacture Test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Step (1) examine the patent-in-suit to determine the article-of-manufacture (the component of the overall device to which the ornamental design was applied); Step (2) ascertain the quantum of damages (profits) that arise from that article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is Samsung’s advocated framework: first identify the component (not necessarily the whole product), then calculate profits attributable to that component. The analysis recognizes components like a phone screen or bezel may be the relevant article-of-manufacture rather than the entire device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Profits calculation — accounting (cost/profit-margin) method
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine profits through ordinary accounting by looking to the cost of the goods sold for the relevant component relative to revenues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine cost of the particular article-of-manufacture to which the patented design was applied, compare with expense of the overall device and the device's profit margin to calculate the profit attributable to the infringing article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Profits calculation — consumer demand evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Use consumer-demand evidence (surveys, expert testimony) to determine how much of the device’s profit is attributable to the patented design/component.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consumer surveys and expert testimony can show the importance of the design to purchasers and thus the share of profits attributable to the infringing article. This method acknowledges that consumer valuation may derive from multiple features beyond ornamentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Samsung’s proposed component-all-profits rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Award all profits for a particular component (article-of-manufacture) even if the design patent does not cover non-design features of that component.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a smartphone screen with patented design plus water/shatter-resistant functional features — Samsung argued all profits on the screen should be awarded, including those from non-design features. Samsung noted this approach is more generous and would grant profits that pure apportionment (which the page says is prohibited by statute) would not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicitor General two-factor test
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) Determine what the article-of-manufacture is; (2) Determine how much of the total profits from the device are attributable to the infringing article-of-manufacture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The SG agreed that the article-of-manufacture may be smaller than the entire product and proposed addressing the second factor (quantifying attributable profits) later; the SG’s framing separates identification of the article from apportionment of profits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicitor General four-factor test for identifying the article-of-manufacture
rubrics_metrics.description: Four factors proposed to determine the article-of-manufacture: (1) compare scope of the patented design as shown in the drawings; (2) determine how prominently that design features in the accused article; (3) determine whether there are other conceptually distinct innovations or components in the article not part of or associated with the patent design; (4) compare the physical relationship between the patented design and the rest of the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factors are intended to guide courts in deciding whether the relevant article is the whole product or a component; they look to claim/drawing scope, prominence to consumers, conceptual distinctness of other parts, and physical unity/separability of the patented design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate error principle — entire product not always the article-of-manufacture
rubrics_metrics.description: It was error for the appellate court to hold that the relevant article-of-manufacture for which profits are owed is always the entire product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both parties and the Solicitor General agreed that the article-of-manufacture can be a component. The Supreme Court was being asked to correct the rule that had automatically equated article-of-manufacture with the whole end product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary requirement: identification and proof of alternative article-of-manufacture to the jury
rubrics_metrics.description: A party seeking non-whole-product damages must present evidence to the jury identifying the alternative article-of-manufacture and calculate profits accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apple argued Samsung never identified to the jury any article other than the phones and Samsung’s expert calculated total profits only on the phones. This highlights that, procedurally, parties must present and support alternative article definitions and profit calculations at trial to obtain non-whole-product remedies on appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative purpose/ deterrence rationale for broad damages
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute’s remedy was intended to deter copying of designs by allowing recovery of full profits rather than small, de minimis sums that would make copying 'the cost of doing business.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apple argued Congress feared that small awards would be inadequate deterrence (example: a 10% profit margin on a $2.50 item). This policy argument supports awarding substantial profits to discourage design copying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation on remedies — no double recovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 289 provides that nothing in the section shall prevent other remedies but the patent owner 'shall not twice recover the profit made from the infringement.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where §289 allows total profit recovery on an article-of-manufacture, courts must ensure the patentee does not obtain duplicative recovery for the same profit through multiple remedies.
